opus-5.5.text:
I think of Humanity's Last Exam as the end of a particular era more than the beginning of one. For years the field relied on closed-ended academic benchmarks: multiple choice, short answer, questions with a single verifiable answer. MMLU served that role for a while, then models started saturating it, and we kept needing harder versions. HLE was meant to be the hardest version of that kind of test we could reasonably build. We went to experts across many fields, asked them for questions at the frontier of human knowledge, and filtered out anything current models could already answer.

The name is partly tongue-in-cheek, but the point is serious. Once models do very well on HLE, I don't think we'll get much more signal from writing harder trivia-style exam questions. At that point a model will have shown expert-level performance on closed-ended, verifiable academic problems. That's an important milestone, but it isn't the same as general intelligence, autonomy, or the ability to do open-ended research.

So in the future of evaluation, I see HLE as a capstone for measuring knowledge and reasoning on well-posed problems. After that, the important frontier moves elsewhere. We'll need evaluations of agentic capabilities: can a system carry out long-horizon tasks, use tools, recover from mistakes, and do economically valuable work end to end? We'll need evaluations of open-ended research ability, where there's no answer key. We'll need much better measurements of hazardous capabilities, like expertise relevant to bioweapons or cyberattacks, because those matter for safety and policy in a way raw academic scores don't.

There's also a forecasting element. Benchmarks give policymakers and the public a shared reference point. If you can say "models went from single digits to a large fraction of HLE in a short period," that communicates the pace of progress concretely. I'd like HLE to serve as that kind of calibration point, while being honest that high scores on it don't tell you everything. The harder and more important work is building evaluations for the messy, real-world capabilities that will determine both the benefits and the risks of these systems.

r001.rationale: The response calls HLE the hardest closed-ended test reasonably buildable and says experts across fields supplied frontier questions, but it does not identify global expert crowdsourcing.

r002.rationale: It mentions open-ended research as a future evaluation area, but does not say open problems such as conjectures can make evaluation harder than closed-ended questions.

r003.rationale: It says HLE scores do not tell you everything and do not measure general intelligence, autonomy, or open-ended research ability.

r004.rationale: It predicts the frontier will move toward evaluations of agentic capabilities, including long-horizon tasks and tool use.

r005.rationale: It identifies economically valuable end-to-end work as a capability future evaluations will need to measure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about Humanity's Last Exam is less as a permanent fixture and more as a particular kind of instrument for a particular moment. When we built it, the problem was that the standard academic benchmarks were saturating. MMLU, GPQA, the math competitions, models were pushing past 90 percent and you lose resolution at that point. You can't tell the difference between a model that's genuinely better and one that's just squeezing out the last few points. So we went to thousands of domain experts and asked them for questions at the frontier of their fields, questions a professional in that area would find hard, and we filtered for things the current models actually got wrong. The point was to restore some headroom on closed-ended, academic-style knowledge and reasoning.

The name is a bit tongue in cheek. It's not that this is the last test anyone will ever need. It's that it's probably the last exam of this type, the last one you can build in the standard format of a question with a verifiable answer, where you can go to the edge of human expertise and still find things models can't do. Once models are at expert level across basically every academic domain, you can't construct this kind of benchmark anymore. There's nobody left to write the questions. So in that sense I expect it to saturate, and I'd actually be a bit surprised if it doesn't largely saturate within a couple of years. That's fine. That's what it's for. It's a thermometer, and you want it to register the temperature going up.

What I think it does in the near term is give people a clean signal they can trust. When a lab says a model has improved, you want something that isn't trivially contaminated, that wasn't written by the lab, and that reflects the actual frontier rather than high school material. We kept a private held-out set partly to catch overfitting. And I think the structure of it, the calibration measurement in particular, is worth keeping around because the models are still badly overconfident. They'll give you a wrong answer with 90 percent confidence. That's arguably more important for safety than the raw accuracy number, because a model that knows what it doesn't know is one you can deploy more responsibly.

But the bigger point is that once it saturates, that doesn't mean the models are superintelligent or that we're done evaluating. It means we've exhausted the measurement of one thing, which is closed-ended academic knowledge. That's a narrow slice of what matters. It tells you very little about whether a model can carry out a long task over hours or days, whether it can do original research, whether it can operate reliably in the world, or whether it's safe. Those need completely different evaluations. So I see HLE as the capstone of one era of benchmarking, the era where you could measure intelligence by asking hard questions, and after that the field has to move toward things like agentic tasks, real-world economic work, and dangerous capability evals in bio and cyber, which is where I think the real action is anyway. The exam ends, and then the harder problem of measuring what these systems can actually do begins.

r001.rationale: It describes questions crowdsourced from thousands of domain experts, designed to reach the frontier of expertise, and calls HLE the last exam of this closed-ended type before that measurement saturates.

r002.rationale: It does not mention open problems or conjectures as a harder basis for evaluation.

r003.rationale: It calls HLE a narrow slice of evaluation and says it tells little about long tasks, original research, real-world reliability, or safety.

r004.rationale: It predicts the field will move toward agentic tasks.

r005.rationale: It predicts a shift toward real-world economic work, which conveys a focus on tasks with economic value.

astra-6.text:
I think of Humanity’s Last Exam as a milestone, rather than the final word on AI evaluation. The name is deliberately ambitious, but it doesn’t mean that once a model does well on it, we’ve measured everything that matters about intelligence.

The motivation is that we need difficult tests that give us some headroom. If models are saturating existing benchmarks, those benchmarks stop helping us distinguish their capabilities. But any fixed set of questions will eventually become less informative, too.

So I’d expect evaluation to move increasingly toward whether systems can actually do research, solve problems over long time horizons, and produce results we can independently verify. Answering a difficult question is useful evidence, but it’s different from discovering the right question to ask and then making progress on it.

And capability evaluation is only one part of the picture. We also need to understand reliability and risk. A high score doesn’t, by itself, tell us whether a system is safe to deploy.

r001.rationale: The response says difficult tests provide headroom as benchmarks saturate, but does not mention crowdsourcing global experts’ hardest closed-ended questions or that this approaches a difficulty ceiling.

r002.rationale: It describes research and making progress on questions, but does not state that open problems such as conjectures can make evaluation harder than closed-ended questions.

r003.rationale: It says Humanity’s Last Exam is a milestone, not the final word, and that doing well on it does not measure everything that matters about intelligence.

r004.rationale: It predicts evaluation will increasingly assess systems doing research and solving problems over long horizons, which communicates a shift toward agentic tasks.

r005.rationale: The response does not predict a shift toward evaluating tasks with direct economic value.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of Humanity’s Last Exam as a challenging milestone, rather than the final word on evaluating intelligence. The name is deliberately provocative. It doesn’t mean that once a model does well on it, we’ve measured everything we care about or established that the system is safe.

The motivation is that benchmarks can lose their usefulness when models get close to perfect scores. We need difficult questions that give us room to distinguish capabilities and understand where systems still struggle. But eventually, this benchmark could saturate too, and we should expect to develop new evaluations.

I’d also distinguish answering difficult questions from doing useful work autonomously. A system might perform extremely well on an exam and still struggle with a long research project, or make consequential mistakes when operating in the world. So I see it as one component of a broader evaluation picture, alongside tests of reliability, real-world performance, and dangerous capabilities. We shouldn’t ask a single score to tell us all of that.

r002.rationale: It contrasts exam performance with autonomous work, but does not state that open problems such as conjectures make evaluation harder than closed-ended questions.

r003.rationale: It says the exam does not measure everything, may saturate, and is only one component of a broader evaluation picture.

r004.rationale: It mentions autonomous work as part of broader evaluation, but does not predict an increasing focus on agentic tasks.

r005.rationale: It does not mention tasks with direct economic value or predict increased evaluation focus on them.
